podcast.title: Band Members' Sobriety (2003)
podcast.body: The members of Velvet Revolver (McKagan, Slash, Sorum, Kushner) were all 100% clean from drugs at the time of their formation, providing a potential environment to help Scott Weiland get clean as well. "And all the other guys had been in trouble with drugs too and were all 100% clean. So maybe this was the environment that would help him get clean too."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Formation as a Supergroup (2003)
podcast.body: Formed in 2003, Velvet Revolver began with former Guns N' Roses members Duff McKagan, Slash, and Matt Sorum, who then recruited Dave Kushner from Wasted Youth. They auditioned several singers, including Josh Todd of Buckcherry, Travis Meeks of Days of the New, and B-Real of Cypress Hill, before settling on Scott Weiland. "Susan told Mary that three guys from Guns and Roses had kissed and made up and were forming a new band."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Movie Soundtrack Debut (2003)
podcast.body: The band's first public music release was a couple of soundtrack songs for "The Hulk" movie in the summer of 2003, approximately a month before Scott Weiland's arrest for heroin possession. "The first anyone ever heard of this new group was via the movie The Hulk, which came out on the summer of 2003."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Scott Weiland's Initial Reluctance and Trust (2003)
podcast.body: Scott Weiland initially disliked the music presented by the band, but a second demo convinced him to jam. He showed up late due to drug use, but found unexpected chemistry and a low ego factor, particularly trusting Matt Sorum due to a shared rehab experience. "Matt, to Scott's surprise, the ego factor was low and the chemistry was bang on. Besides, he'd been in rehab with Matt Sorom so he trusted him."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Scott Weiland's Rehab Before Debut Album (2003)
podcast.body: Prior to recording their debut album, Scott Weiland underwent another trip to rehab to get straight. When that proved insufficient, Duff McKagan arranged for him to train with a martial arts expert in Washington state, which helped Weiland achieve sobriety and health. "First there was another trip to rehab to straighten out a bit before the band got to work on their debut album."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: DUI Charge (2004)
podcast.body: In July 2004, Scott Weiland was charged with DUI and sentenced to three months probation and a six-month rehab program. "In July 2004 he was charged with DUI in sentenced to 3 months probation in a 6 month rehab program."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Longevity Beyond Expectations (2004-2009)
podcast.body: Despite initial skepticism about their durability (many doubted they would last more than one album and tour), Velvet Revolver remained together for five years and released two albums. "No one wanted to bet on this band lasting more than one album and one tour. That however turned out to be wrong. Velvara Volver held it together for five years in two albums."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Manufactured Supergroup (2004)
podcast.body: Velvet Revolver was openly acknowledged as a "manufactured product" assembled by managers, essentially a combination of Guns N' Roses members with Scott Weiland and another musician, rather than a naturally formed group. "It was a manufactured product put together as a supergroup by various managers. It was basically guns and roses with Scott Wyland and some other guy."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Tense Press Conference Dynamics (2004)
podcast.body: At a press conference for the "Contraband" album, the former Guns N' Roses members (Duff, Slash, Matt) were friendly and engaging, while Dave Kushner was quiet. Scott Weiland, however, was totally separate, aloof, and unapproachable, creating palpable tension and doubt about the band's longevity. "He exhibited an aloofness that resulted in a puppable tension when he was in the room. And while the rest of the band was only too happy to talk, Wyland was icy cold and completely unapproachable."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Weiland's DUI and Rehab (July 2004)
podcast.body: In July 2004, Scott Weiland was charged with DUI and sentenced to three months probation and a six-month rehab program. "In July 2004, he was charged with DUI and sentenced to three months probation into a six-month rehab program."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Weiland's DUI and Rehab (July 2004)
podcast.body: In July 2004, Scott Weiland was charged with DUI and sentenced to three months probation and a six-month rehab program. "In July 2004 he was charged with DUI in sentenced to 3 months probation in a 6 month rehab program."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Tour Cancellations (2006-2007)
podcast.body: A tour of Japan was cancelled because Velvet Revolver was denied visas, attributed to Scott Weiland's legal attention. A tour of Australia was also called off, after which Weiland "voluntarily went into rehab." "A tour of Japan was cancelled because Velvet Revolver was denied visas. Guess who cut the attention of the authorities?"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Rough Start to 2007
podcast.body: The year 2007 began difficult for the band with the death of Matt Sorum's younger brother from brain cancer in early March, followed by the death of Scott Weiland's younger brother, Michael, a month later. "Things started off rough for Velvara Volver in 2007. Former Matt Sorum's little brother died of brain cancer the first week of March."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Second DUI Charge (2007)
podcast.body: In November 2007, a supposedly sober Scott Weiland was caught on another DUI charge, resulting in an 18-month alcohol rehab program, four years probation, and an eight-day jail sentence (though he served only 10 hours). "A supposedly sober Wyland was caught on another DUI charge and sentenced to 18 months in an alcohol rehab program, four years probation and eight days in jail."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Tour Cancellations Due to Scott Weiland's DUI (2007)
podcast.body: Scott Weiland's DUI arrest on November 21, 2007, caused a "disaster" for Velvet Revolver, leading to the cancellation of many dates on their international tour for the "Libertad" album. Japan refused the band entry, and Australia dates were cancelled. "Japan refused the band entry outright. Australia was canceled."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Band Estrangement and Public Announcement (2008)
podcast.body: During a UK tour in early 2008, no one in the band was speaking with Scott Weiland due to his backsliding drug use. At a Glasgow gig on March 20, 2008, Weiland "announced to the crowd that this was the band's last tour," surprising the rest of the band. "When the road trip got to the UK nobody in the band was speaking with him."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Band's Financial Demands on Scott Weiland (2008)
podcast.body: Following the extensive tour cancellations caused by Scott Weiland's DUI, the other band members were "pissed" and demanded that Weiland reimburse them out of his own pocket for all the lost revenue, which further strained internal relations. "They demanded that since this was Scott's fault, that he reimburse all of them for the lost revenue out of his own pocket."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: End with Scott Weiland (April 1, 2008)
podcast.body: Velvet Revolver's final gig with Scott Weiland as their singer took place in Amsterdam on April 1, 2008, effectively marking the end of his tenure with the band. "So velvet revolver was done, at least with Scott as their singer."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Scott Weiland Declares Band's End (March 20, 2008)
podcast.body: Angered by the financial demands, Scott Weiland unilaterally announced to the crowd at a Glasgow gig on March 20, 2008, that it would be the "last ever Velvet Revolver tour." The band performed eight more shows, with their final gig in Amsterdam on April 1, 2008. "Scott was so angry that on March 20, 2008, during a gig at the Carling Academy in Glasgow, and he unilaterally announced to the crowd that this was the last ever velvet revolver tour."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Scott Weiland's Departure (March 21, 2008)
podcast.body: Scott Weiland announced mid-show that this tour would be his last with Velvet Revolver, a surprise to his bandmates. "On March 21st, 2008, Wyland announced in the middle of a Velvet Revolver show that this would be his last tour with the band."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Scott Weiland's Firing (2008)
podcast.body: Velvet Revolver fired Scott Weiland on April 1, 2008, after his public announcement about the band's last tour. Weiland countered, claiming he was "ousted by a bunch of Eagle Maniacs." "Didn't matter though because the band was planning to fire him anyway, which they did on April 1st 2008."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Scott Weiland's Firing (April 1, 2008)
podcast.body: Velvet Revolver fired Scott Weiland on April 1, 2008, after a series of "crazy antics" during a tour through the UK. Weiland responded by claiming he was ousted by "a bunch of egomaniacs." "Velvet Revolver got fed up with him and fired Wyland on April 1, 2008, after a bunch of crazy antics on a swing through the UK."

podcast.title: Talk of Returning to Velvet Revolver (Circa 2010)
podcast.body: After a period of stability for Scott Weiland around 2010, there was discussion about a potential return to Velvet Revolver, but the band ultimately did not want him back due to his continued struggles with addiction. "And there was talk about returning to Velvet Revolver. And frankly neither did STP. As far as they were concerned, Wylin had gone back to his old ways."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Band Members' Personality
podcast.body: Ian Thorneley found the members of Velvet Revolver, including Slash, to be "really, really sweet and articulate and cool and down to earth," akin to any other band members he had toured with. "They were just like real dudes. They were real normal guys like any other band that I toured with before."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Ian Thornley - In His Own Words: Part 2

podcast.title: Brilliant Beginning, Debacle End
podcast.body: Velvet Revolver's story was characterized by a brilliant start but ended in a "debacle," which was attributed almost entirely to Scott Weiland's issues. "The whole Velvet Revolver story, which began so brilliantly and ended in such a debacle, thanks almost entirely to Scott."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Ian Thorneley's Audition Experience
podcast.body: Ian Thorneley rehearsed with Velvet Revolver in Los Angeles after Scott Weiland's departure. He found the musical aspect and chemistry to be strong, and the band members (Slash, Duff McKagan, etc.) to be "real dudes" and normal guys, contrary to any "reality show" perception. "It was really nice to see that. It wasn't, it wasn't the reality show, whatever that I had imagined it would be like."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Ian Thornley - In His Own Words: Part 2

podcast.title: Inability to Replace Weiland
podcast.body: After Scott Weiland's departure, Velvet Revolver was unable to find a suitable replacement for him despite numerous attempts, effectively leading to the end of the band. "In any event, that was definitely the end of Velvet Revolver because despite trying and trying and trying, they couldn't find a replacement for Wyland."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Longevity (Three Years)
podcast.body: Despite the challenges of managing "all those egos," the band managed to last for "two albums and a bunch of tours over three years." "Managing all those egos in town must have been tough and it's amazing they lasted for two albums at a bunch of tours over three years."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Scott Weiland's Involvement and Behavior
podcast.body: Velvet Revolver was Scott Weiland's project after the initial breakup of Stone Temple Pilots. He was described as a "pain in the ass" to this group as well. "Wyland's next project was Velvet Revolver. He was a pin in the ass to them too."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Scott Weiland's Post-STP Project
podcast.body: After Stone Temple Pilots' 2002 breakup, Scott Weiland joined Velvet Revolver as their singer from 2004 to 2008. He either quit or was fired after two albums. "Wyland went on to join Velvet Revolver as their singer between 2004 and 2008."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Groups That Changed Their Front-Person and Survived

podcast.title: Search for a New Vocalist
podcast.body: Velvet Revolver sought a new lead singer on two separate occasions: once before Scott Weiland joined, and again after his departure. Ian Thorneley was considered during both searches. "Looking for a guided replace Scott W Island. And somehow your name came up. So let's go through that story because I find this is fascinating."

podcast.body: Duff McKagan joined Velvet Revolver as the bass player after he had become clean and sober following a life-threatening incident where his pancreas exploded. "Now at revolver, featuring bass player Duff MacKagan, who has been clean and sober ever since his pancreas exploded."

podcast.title: Video Appearance
podcast.body: Slash, Duff McKagan, and Matt Sorum, who were also members of Velvet Revolver (and Guns N' Roses), appeared in The Strokes' music video for "Someday." This collaboration was noted as a significant endorsement for the emerging band. "They even had Slash, Duff McKagan and Matt Soren from Guns and Roses and Velvet Revolver appear in their video."

"While driving somewhere in Hollywood after midnight, Scott hit a parked car. He was arrested again and sent to what's called residential rehab to detox yet again."

xref.title: Reconciliation and Reunion Tour (2008)
xref.body: Following Scott Weiland's departure from Velvet Revolver, Mary Forsberg organized a party featuring the DeLeo brothers where a "big reconciliation" occurred, leading to Stone Temple Pilots' return. xref.title: Scott Weiland Quits Velvet Revolver (March 21, 2008)
xref.body: Weiland surprised his Velvet Revolver bandmates by announcing mid-show that this would be his last tour with them, freeing him up for a potential STP reunion. "On March 21st, 2008, Wyland announced in the middle of a Velvet Revolver show that this would be his last tour with the band."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Reunions: Some Lasted....and Sadly, Some Didn't ｜ Part 1

xref.title: Unilateral Announcement of Velvet Revolver End (March 20, 2008)
xref.body: In a fit of anger over his bandmates' demands for reimbursement after his DUI-related tour cancellations, Scott Weiland unilaterally announced to the crowd at a gig at the Carling Academy in Glasgow on March 20, 2008, that it was the "last ever Velvet Revolver tour." "Scott was so angry that on March 20, 2008, during a gig at the Carling Academy in Glasgow, and he unilaterally announced to the crowd that this was the last ever velvet revolver tour."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Decades of Personal Problems
xref.body: Scott Weiland's life was marked by decades of insurmountable personal problems, including severe drug abuse, repeated failed rehab attempts, DUIs, jail time, mental illness (bipolar disorder), intermittent band membership, marital issues, and co-dependencies. These issues ultimately contributed to his early demise. "Behind it all, though, were decades of insurmountable personal problems. Drug abuse, the rehab stints that never took, the DUIs, jail, the mental illness, the on-again off-again membership in STP, the brawling egos and velvet revolver, the bad marriages, the co-dependencies."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: First Velvet Revolver Consideration (Pre-Weiland)
xref.body: Before Scott Weiland joined Velvet Revolver, Ian Thorneley was considered as a potential singer. He received a CD with three instrumental tracks to write over, but he didn't pay much attention to it as his first Thorneley record was about to be released. "I remember getting a CD right before the first Thorneley record came out. I got a CD with three cuts on it, just instrumental tracks."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Ian Thornley - In His Own Words: Part 2

xref.title: Reason for Rejecting Velvet Revolver Frontman Role
xref.body: Despite the musical chemistry and positive vibe during rehearsals, Ian Thorneley ultimately did not join Velvet Revolver. The band sought a "peacock" frontman in the vein of David Lee Roth or Scott Weiland, a role that didn't align with Ian's preference to play guitar on stage. "I'm not that comfortable doing the whole, you know, front guy tambourine thing. It's just not for me."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Ian Thornley - In His Own Words: Part 2

xref.title: Second Velvet Revolver Consideration and Rehearsals (Post-Weiland)
xref.body: After Scott Weiland's departure, Ian was again approached by Velvet Revolver. Slash himself called Ian to send over material, and Ian subsequently rehearsed with the band in Los Angeles, experiencing Slash's full touring rig and observing the band members as "real dudes." "The phone call came from slash. I was driving back from a gig or something. Oh, the phone rings and it's slash."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Ian Thornley - In His Own Words: Part 2

xref.title: Velvet Revolver Audition
xref.body: Ian Thornley was offered the opportunity to become the lead singer and frontman for Velvet Revolver on two separate occasions. "he was offered the opportunity to become the lead singer in frontman for Velvet Revolver."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Ian Thornley - In His Own Words: Part 1

xref.title: Video Appearance
xref.body: Slash, Duff McKagan, and Matt Sorum from Guns N' Roses and Velvet Revolver made an appearance in The Strokes' music video for their song "Someday," the third single from their debut album "Is This It." "They even had Slash, Duff McKagan and Matt Soren from Guns and Roses and Velvet Revolver appear in their video."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Weiland Joins Velvet Revolver (Post-STP)
xref.body: Scott Weiland joined Velvet Revolver, formed with ex-Guns N' Roses members, which released two albums and toured for three years, managing "all those egos." "Meanwhile, Wyland ended up in Velvet Revolver with the ex-Gunz and Roses guys. And they did pretty well for two albums."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
